p: John opens with the first words of the Bible, and then goes back before creation.
b: The Greek en archē is exactly how the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, begins Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). John's readers would hear Genesis at once, and the echoes keep coming: light, darkness, life, and everything coming to be through God's word (1:3–5). But Genesis starts with creation, and John starts earlier. At the beginning the Word already "was" (the Greek imperfect, ēn, pictures ongoing existence), before anything "came to exist" (egeneto, 1:3). The contrast between "was" and "came to be" runs through the whole prologue.

p: Logos meant word, reason and message. Greeks, Jews and Christians each heard something in it.
b: Logos means a spoken word, a message, or the reason behind things. Greek thinkers such as Heraclitus and the Stoics used it for the reason that orders the universe. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of Jesus' day, called the Logos God's image and agent in creation, even "the firstborn" and "a second god". The Hebrew Bible says the heavens were made "by the LORD's word" (Psalm 33:6), and Lady Wisdom stood beside God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31; compare Wisdom of Solomon 9:1–2). The Targums, the Aramaic paraphrases read in synagogues, often say God acted through his Memra, his "Word". Most scholars think John draws above all on the Jewish Scriptures and Wisdom, while choosing a term Greek readers also understood.
r: Psalm 33:6; Psalm 107:20; Proverbs 8:22–31; Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 John 1:1; Revelation 19:13

p: The Greek preposition suggests closeness and relationship, not just being in the same place.
b: John does not use the usual Greek word for "with" (meta or para) but pros, which normally means "toward". With a verb of being it means "in the company of", as in Mark 6:3 ("And his sisters are here among us, aren't they?"). Many readers, from the church fathers to modern commentators, hear in it a picture of the Word turned toward God, in close relationship. Grammarians warn not to press the preposition too far, but the clause plainly sets the Word apart from God the Father ("with God") just before the next clause says the Word "was God". John holds both together.

p: Theos here has no article. Does that make it "a god", "divine", or "God"? Grammar and history weigh in.
b: The Greek is theos ēn ho logos: "God was the Word", with no article before theos. Greek has no word for "a", and the article marks the subject: "the Word". Had John written ho theos, he would have said the Word is the same as the God he was "with", the Father. Leaving off the article lets theos describe what the Word is (Philip Harner calls it "qualitative"): the Word has the nature of God, or as some render it, "what God was, the Word was". The New World Translation of Jehovah's Witnesses reads "the Word was a god", a lesser divine being. Most grammarians reply that John uses theos without the article for the one God elsewhere (1:6, 12, 13, 18), and that Jewish monotheism left no room for a second "god". Unitarian and Christadelphian readers take another path: the Word is God's own plan or utterance, personified, which "became flesh" when Jesus was born, so the Word was God in the sense that a person's word is the person speaking. See the card below.
orig: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος (theos ēn ho logos)

a: Through him everything came to exist
p: Jews said God created through his word and his wisdom. John names that agent as a person.
b: In Genesis 1 God speaks and things come to be. Proverbs pictures Wisdom at God's side as "a craftsman" (Proverbs 8:30), and the Wisdom of Solomon prays to God "who made all things by your word" (Wisdom of Solomon 9:1). John says the Word was the one "through" whom all things came into being, without exception. Paul and Hebrews say the same of Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). The early church used this verse against teachers who said a lesser god made the material world: nothing at all came to be without the Word.
r: Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6; Proverbs 8:30; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2

p: Light and life go together from Genesis on. In John, Jesus will say "I am the light of the world."
b: God's first word in Genesis made light (Genesis 1:3), and the Psalms say, "in your light we see light" (Psalm 36:9). Here the Word's life is the light people live by. The pair returns across the Gospel: Jesus calls himself the light of the world (8:12; 9:5), gives sight to a man born blind (9), and warns about walking in darkness (12:35–36). The Dead Sea Scrolls also speak of "sons of light" and "sons of darkness", which shows that this way of talking was at home in Jewish Palestine and need not come from Greek philosophy.

a: did not get hold of it
p: The Greek verb can mean "seize" or "grasp with the mind." The KJV says "comprehended"; many modern Bibles say "overcome."
b: Katelaben means to take hold of something. It can mean to seize or overpower (as in 12:35, of darkness overtaking people) or to grasp with the mind (Acts 10:34). The KJV took it as "the darkness comprehended it not": people did not understand the light. Many modern translations take it as "overcome": darkness tried to put out the light and failed, a hint of the cross and the resurrection. Some think John meant both, as he often uses words with two meanings. This translation uses "get hold of", which keeps both senses open.

p: This Gospel never calls him "the Baptist." To John the Evangelist, he is simply the witness.
b: The other Gospels call him "John the Baptist". This Gospel just says "John", and it never names the apostle John at all, which some take as a clue to its author. John son of Zechariah preached repentance and immersed people in the Jordan. The Jewish historian Josephus also describes him as a good man who urged Jews to practice justice and piety and to be baptized, and says Herod Antipas killed him for fear of an uprising (Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119). In this Gospel John's whole role is to testify about Jesus (1:7–8, 15, 19–36; 3:27–30; 5:33–35; 10:41).

p: John's Gospel reads like a trial. "Testify" and "testimony" appear about 47 times.
b: The verb martyreō, "testify, bear witness", and the noun martyria, "testimony", come up more in John than in the rest of the Gospels together. A series of witnesses speaks for Jesus: John the Baptist, the Samaritan woman (4:39), Jesus' works, the Scriptures and the Father (5:31–39), the Spirit and the disciples (15:26–27), and the disciple who wrote the book (19:35; 21:24). Many scholars see the Gospel as a kind of trial in which the world judges Jesus, and the reader is the jury. Our word "martyr" comes from the same Greek root.

p: The Greek can mean the light was coming into the world, or that it lights everyone who comes into the world.
b: The participle "coming" (erchomenon) can go with "the light" or with "every person". The KJV took it the second way: the light "lighteth every man that cometh into the world". Most modern scholars take it the first way, since John often speaks of Jesus "coming into the world" (3:19; 6:14; 11:27; 12:46). The adjective alēthinos means "real, genuine", the true thing that other lights only point to, as in "the real bread" (6:32) and "the real vine" (15:1). Quakers have long read this verse as the "inward light" given to every person.
orig: τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν ... ἐρχόμενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον

a: his own people did not welcome him
t: His own: Israel, or all people?
p: "His own" may mean the world the Word made, or Israel, his own people. The verse is not a verdict on all Jews.
b: The Greek has a neuter, "his own things" or "his own home", then a masculine, "his own people". Many read it of Israel: the Messiah came to his own nation, and its leaders did not receive him. Others read it of humanity: the Word came into the world he made (1:10). Either way, the next verses show that some did receive him, and the first who did were Jews: John, Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael. Reading 1:11 as God's rejection of the Jewish people misuses it.

p: John never uses the noun "faith." He uses the verb "believe" about 98 times, usually "believe into" someone.
b: Paul and the other Gospels often speak of pistis, "faith". John never uses the noun. Instead he uses the verb pisteuō, "believe, trust", about 98 times, often with eis, "into": not only believing that something is true, but putting one's trust into a person. "His name" stands for the person himself, as in the Hebrew Bible. The Gospel's stated purpose is that readers keep believing and have life in his name (20:31).
orig: τοῖς πιστεύουσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ

p: John calls believers God's "children" (tekna); he keeps "Son" (huios) for Jesus alone.
b: Paul calls believers God's "sons" by adoption (Romans 8:14–15; Galatians 4:5–7). John's Gospel and letters never do. Believers are tekna theou, God's children, born from him (1:13; 3:3–8; 1 John 3:1–2), while Jesus alone is "the Son". The right to become God's children is a gift ("he gave"), not a birthright. Israel had been called God's son (Exodus 4:22), and this gift now opens to all who believe.

a: Their birth came not from blood
t: Blood, flesh and a man's decision
p: Ancient people thought a child formed from the mother's blood and the father's seed. John lists every human cause.
b: "Blood" is plural in Greek ("bloods"), perhaps because ancient medicine held that a child formed from the mixing of the mother's blood with the father's seed (Wisdom of Solomon 7:2 says the writer was "compacted with blood"). "Fleshly desire" (literally "the will of the flesh") is human sexual desire, and "a man's decision" is literally "the will of a man": anēr means a male, often a husband, so the phrase points to the father's choice. John piles up every human cause of birth to deny them all: God's children are born from God. A few early writers read this verse as being about Jesus' own virgin birth (see the variant).

p: Not "took on a body" or "appeared in" flesh: the Word became flesh, weak and mortal human life.
b: Sarx, "flesh", in the Bible often means human life in its weakness and mortality (Isaiah 40:6, "all flesh is grass"). John could have said the Word "took a body" or "appeared as a man". He says the Word became flesh. Some early Christians (called Docetists, from Greek dokeō, "to seem") taught that Christ only seemed to be human, and 1 John answers that every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ "come in the flesh" is from God (1 John 4:2). The creeds speak of the Son "incarnate", from the Latin for "in flesh". In many churches people kneel or bow at these words in the Creed.

p: The verb means "to live in a tent." It recalls the tabernacle, where God's glory lived among Israel.
b: Eskēnōsen comes from skēnē, "tent", the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tabernacle. God told Moses, "They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst" (Exodus 25:8), and when it was finished "the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). Sirach has Wisdom say that God told her, "pitch your tent in Jacob" (Sirach 24:8). The Greek letters s-k-n also echo the Hebrew shakan, "to dwell", from which the rabbis made Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence. John says that presence now lived among people in a human life.

p: "We" may be eyewitnesses, the whole church, or both. John has no transfiguration story; the glory is seen all through.
b: Etheasametha means "we looked at, we saw for ourselves". Many read "we" as eyewitnesses, as in 1 John 1:1 ("what we have seen with our eyes") and John 21:24. Others think the voice is the believing community, who "see" by faith what the first disciples saw. In the other Gospels three disciples see Jesus' glory on a mountain (Mark 9:2–8); John never tells that story. In this Gospel glory shows in the signs (2:11), and above all on the cross, where Jesus is "glorified" (12:23; 17:1).

a: the kind of glory an only son has from his father
p: Monogenēs means "one of a kind, only." The KJV's "only begotten" comes from the Latin, not the Greek.
b: Monogenēs combines monos, "only", with a root meaning "kind" (genos), not "begotten" (gennaō). It is used for an only child (Luke 7:12; 8:42; 9:38) and for Isaac, Abraham's unique son of promise, though Abraham had others (Hebrews 11:17). Jerome's Latin rendered it unigenitus, "only begotten", in the creed-shaped passages, and the KJV followed. The RSV (1946) said "only Son", and Dale Moody's article (1953) defended that choice; most later translations say "only" or "one and only". A minority still defends a sense of "begotten" (Charles Lee Irons, 2017), linking the word to birth from a father. The Nicene Creed's "begotten of the Father before all ages" rests on other grounds too, and the new rendering does not deny it. Here there is no article in Greek and the word "from" (para) is used: "glory as of an only son from a father". This translation takes it as a comparison, the kind of glory an only son receives from his father, while the next verses make clear that the only Son is Jesus and the Father is God (1:18). Many translations instead write "the only Son from the Father".

t: Grace and truth: the God of Sinai
p: This pair echoes God's name in Exodus 34:6: "great in loyal love and faithfulness."
b: When Moses asked to see God's glory, the LORD passed by and proclaimed himself "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The Hebrew pair chesed ("loyal love") and emet ("faithfulness, truth") stands behind John's "grace and truth". John is saying that the glory Moses could not see face to face (Exodus 33:20) has now been seen in the Word made flesh. The next verses keep the Exodus story in view: Moses, the law, and the claim that no one has seen God (1:17–18).

p: John was born before Jesus (Luke 1:36), yet says Jesus "was before me": a claim about where Jesus came from.
b: The saying plays on time. "Coming after me" means Jesus appears later, as a follower would walk behind a teacher. "Has gone ahead of me" (emprosthen mou gegonen) means he now outranks John. "Because he existed before me" (prōtos mou ēn, "he was first of me") gives the reason. Luke says John was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:36), so this is not about birth order. The prologue has already given the answer: the Word was there "in the beginning" (1:1). John says the same in 1:30.

p: The little Greek word anti means "in place of." What grace replaces what? Three main answers.
b: Charin anti charitos, literally "grace instead of grace". (1) Grace upon grace: one gift after another, wave upon wave, the most common modern reading, though anti rarely means "upon". (2) Replacement: the grace given through Moses (the law, 1:17) is replaced by the grace that came through Jesus Christ; many church fathers, such as John Chrysostom, read it so. (3) Correspondence: grace in Christ matches the grace of God's covenant faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). Whatever the exact sense, the law is not called bad: it too was a gift.

a: through Moses that the law was given
p: There is no "but" in the Greek. John sets Moses and Jesus side by side, not as enemies.
b: Many English Bibles add "but" (KJV "but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ"), which can make the verse sound like law against grace. The Greek simply sets the two clauses side by side. In John, Moses is a true witness who "wrote about" Jesus (1:45; 5:46), and the law is God's gift. What is new is that the grace and truth God showed Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6) now "arrived", took human form, in Jesus Christ. Jewish readers note that Judaism has always called the Torah itself God's gift of grace. This is also the first time the Gospel names "Jesus Christ".

p: God told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive." Yet Jacob, Moses and Isaiah "saw" God. How?
b: God told Moses, "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Yet Jacob said, "I have seen God face to face" (Genesis 32:30), and Isaiah saw the Lord on his throne (Isaiah 6:1). Jewish interpreters solved this in different ways: people saw God's glory, or an angel, or a vision, not God himself. John's answer is that every seeing of God came through the Son: Isaiah saw "his glory" (12:41), and Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9). Many church fathers read the Old Testament appearances of God as the Word before he became flesh.

p: Kolpos is the chest or lap, where a loved one leans at a meal. The Beloved Disciple will lie at Jesus' chest.
b: Kolpos means the chest, bosom or lap. At a banquet people reclined on couches, and the guest of honor leaned against the host's chest. The word returns at the last supper, where the disciple Jesus loved reclines "at Jesus' chest" (13:23). As the Son is close to the Father and makes him known, so the Beloved Disciple is close to Jesus and makes him known to the readers. The KJV's "in the bosom of the Father" keeps the image; "at the Father's side" loses some of its warmth.
orig: εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός (eis ton kolpon tou patros)

p: The verb gives us "exegesis." Jesus is the one who explains, narrates and leads God out into view.
b: Exēgēsato literally means "led out". It was used for telling a story in detail (Luke 24:35; Acts 15:12) and for explaining sacred things, as priests and interpreters explained omens and laws. From it comes the English "exegesis", explaining a text. The Greek has no object ("has explained"), so translations supply "him". The point closes the prologue: the God no one has seen is made known by the one who is closest to him. The rest of the Gospel is that explanation.

p: Here "the Jews" are the Jerusalem authorities who send priests. Everyone in the scene, John included, is Jewish.
b: This is the first time the Gospel uses hoi Ioudaioi, "the Jews", and it does so about seventy times. Here it plainly means the leaders in Jerusalem, who can send priests and Levites on an official errand; 1:24 adds that they came from the Pharisees. Some translations write "the Jewish leaders" here. This site keeps "the Jews", as the Greek has it, so readers can see the word and judge each use, and explains each place. Sometimes it means Judeans, sometimes the people as a whole (2:6, 13), and sometimes those hostile to Jesus. The Gospel's harsh uses were later turned against all Jews, a misuse the Second Vatican Council rejected (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965).

p: Priests and Levites were experts in purity rules. A man immersing crowds in the Jordan raised purity questions.
b: Priests served at the altar, and Levites assisted in the Temple. Both knew the rules of washing and purity. John's baptism was an immersion, like the washings Jews used for purity, but done once and tied to repentance before God's coming. That, and the crowds, made him a matter for Jerusalem. The questions ("Who are you?", "What are you baptizing for?") are an official inquiry. This is the only place in John where Levites appear, and the only one in the Gospels where they act in the story (Luke 10:32 has a Levite in a parable).

p: Messiah is Hebrew for "anointed one", Christ in Greek. In John's day hopes for him took many forms.
b: Christos translates the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one". In the Hebrew Bible kings and priests were anointed with oil. By Jesus' day many Jews hoped for an anointed king from David's line (Psalms of Solomon 17), and the Dead Sea Scrolls speak of two anointed ones, a priest and a king. Luke says that people wondered whether John might be the Messiah (Luke 3:15), and a group around John may have honored him highly long after (Acts 19:1–7). John's flat denial ("I am not") may answer them; he says it again in 3:28.

p: Malachi promised Elijah before the day of the LORD. Jesus says John is Elijah (Matthew 11:14); John says he is not.
b: Malachi ends with God's promise to send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5–6). Elijah had been taken up alive (2 Kings 2:11), so many expected him back in person. In Matthew, Jesus says that John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), and Luke says John came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Here John denies it. Readers reconcile this in several ways: John denies being Elijah literally returned; or John did not know his own role; or this Gospel, which keeps every title for Jesus, plays John down on purpose. Jews still set a cup and open the door for Elijah at the Passover Seder.
r: Malachi 4:5–6; 2 Kings 2:11; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10–13; Luke 1:17; Mark 9:11–13

p: Moses promised that God would raise up "a prophet like me." Many expected one special prophet at the end.
b: In Deuteronomy Moses says, "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers. You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). By Jesus' time some Jews expected a single end-time Prophet. A Dead Sea Scroll, 4QTestimonia, sets this verse beside prophecies of a star and a priest, and the Samaritans waited for the Taheb, "the one who returns", a Moses-like figure (see 4:25). In John the crowds later ask whether Jesus is "the Prophet" (6:14; 7:40). Acts says Jesus fulfilled Deuteronomy 18 (Acts 3:22).

p: John quotes Isaiah from the Greek version: "a voice of one shouting in the wilderness."
b: Isaiah 40 begins the prophecies of comfort for exiles: God will lead his people home across the desert. In the Hebrew the voice calls, "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD"; the Greek Septuagint, which John follows, makes "in the wilderness" describe where the voice is. The other three Gospels apply the verse to John (Mark 1:3), but only here does John say it about himself. The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls used the same verse to explain why it had gone into the desert to study the law (Community Rule, 1QS 8:13–16). As always on this site, the Greek kyrios is "the Lord", though Isaiah's Hebrew has the divine name.

a: The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees
p: The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law, with traditions of their own.
b: The Pharisees (perhaps from Hebrew perushim, "separated ones") were a Jewish movement known for exact keeping of the law, including purity and tithing, and for their "traditions of the elders". Josephus says they were the most respected teachers among the people. After the Temple fell in AD 70, their heirs, the rabbis, shaped Judaism. In John they are often paired with the chief priests as a ruling body (7:32; 11:47), which may reflect the writer's own time. The Greek here lacks an article and could mean "some Pharisees had also been sent"; most read it as identifying the senders.

p: Jews washed for purity often. John's immersion was once, for repentance, and pointed ahead to another baptism.
b: Baptizō means to dip or immerse. Jews used stepped pools (mikva'ot), found by the hundreds in Judea, to wash away ritual impurity, and the Dead Sea community bathed daily. Later sources describe the immersion of converts to Judaism. John's baptism differed: it was a single act, in the river, tied to repentance and to the coming judgment (Mark 1:4). John says his water points to someone greater, who "baptizes in the Holy Spirit" (1:33). John's Gospel never actually narrates Jesus' baptism.

p: Untying a master's sandals was the lowest task of a slave. John says he is not worthy even of that.
b: In the ancient world servants untied and carried their master's sandals and washed their feet. A later Jewish saying lists all the tasks a disciple should do for his teacher, as a slave does for a master, except untying his sandal, which was too degrading (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 96a). John says he is not worthy even to be that slave. The Gospel will turn this around: Jesus himself takes a slave's place and washes his disciples' feet (13:4–5).

t: Where was Bethany beyond the Jordan?
p: Not the Bethany near Jerusalem. Its location is unknown; a site east of the Jordan near Jericho is the main candidate.
b: This Bethany is set apart from the village of Martha, Mary and Lazarus near Jerusalem (11:1, 18). Origen (about AD 230) could not find it and preferred "Bethabara", a place shown in his day (see the variant). Christian pilgrims since the 300s have been led to a site on the east bank opposite Jericho, and remains of churches and pools have been excavated at Wadi el-Kharrar in Jordan. Rainer Riesner proposed instead that "Bethany" here means Batanea, the region of Bashan far to the north-east, which would fit the day's walk to Galilee in 1:43. The question is open.

p: Passover lamb, sacrifice, Isaiah's silent servant, or a conquering lamb? Readers have heard all four.
b: No Jewish text before John uses the exact title "Lamb of God", so readers ask which lamb John means. (1) The Passover lamb: in this Gospel Jesus dies when the Passover lambs were killed, and no bone of his is broken (19:14, 36; Exodus 12:46). (2) The daily sacrifice: "two yearling lambs, every day" (Exodus 29:38). (3) The servant of Isaiah, "like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7), who "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). (4) A leader lamb: 1 Enoch's animal vision and Revelation picture a ram or Lamb who conquers (Revelation 5:6; 17:14); C. H. Dodd argued for this. Many also hear Abraham's words, "God will see to the lamb" (Genesis 22:8). John may mean more than one.
r: Exodus 12:3–13; Exodus 12:46; Exodus 29:38–42; Isaiah 53:7; Isaiah 53:12; Genesis 22:8; 19:36; 1 Peter 1:19; Revelation 5:6; 1 Corinthians 5:7

a: the one who takes the world's sin away
p: The verb means both "lift and carry" and "take away." "Sin" is singular: the world's whole burden.
b: Airō means to lift up, carry, or remove. A sacrifice bears sin and takes it away; Isaiah's servant "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12, with a different verb in the Greek). "Sin" is singular, the world's sin as one great weight, not a list of wrongs. "The world" is wide: not Israel only, but all people. In the Latin Mass this line became the Agnus Dei, "Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us."
orig: ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου

p: John does not tell the story of Jesus' baptism; he only reports what he saw. Why a dove?
b: The other Gospels tell how Jesus was baptized and the Spirit came down "like a dove" (Mark 1:10). John's Gospel tells only what John saw and what it meant. The dove may recall the Spirit who "fluttered over the face of the waters" at creation (Genesis 1:2): a Jewish teacher, Ben Zoma, said the Spirit hovered over the waters "like a dove" (Babylonian Talmud, Chagigah 15a). Others think of the dove Noah sent out after the flood, a sign of a new world (Genesis 8:8–12), or of Israel pictured as a dove (Hosea 7:11).

p: Menō, "stay", is one of John's favorite words: the Spirit stays on Jesus; disciples stay with him.
b: The verb menō means to stay, remain, live or abide. John uses it about forty times. The Spirit comes down and stays on Jesus (1:32–33); two disciples ask where Jesus is "staying", and they "stay" with him (1:38–39). Later Jesus tells his disciples to "remain in me" like branches in a vine (15:4–10). This translation uses "stay" in chapter 1 to keep the link visible. The prophets promised that God's Spirit would "rest" on the coming king (Isaiah 11:2).

a: he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit
p: The prophets promised God would pour out his Spirit. Churches differ on when and how believers receive it.
b: The prophets promised that God would wash his people and pour out his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). John contrasts his water with Jesus' gift of the Spirit, given after the resurrection (7:39; 20:22). Christians read "baptism in the Spirit" differently. Many Pentecostal churches teach that it is an experience after conversion, shown by speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4). Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches link the gift of the Spirit with baptism and confirmation or chrismation. Reformed and Baptist churches teach that every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13).

p: Isaiah's servant is God's chosen one, with God's Spirit on him: it fits a verse about the Spirit coming down.
b: If "Chosen One" is the original reading (see the variant), John echoes the first song of the LORD's servant in Isaiah: "He is my chosen one; my soul is pleased with him. I have placed my Spirit on him" (Isaiah 42:1). John has just seen the Spirit come down and stay on Jesus. Luke uses "the Chosen One" for Jesus at the transfiguration and the cross (Luke 9:35; 23:35), and 1 Enoch's Book of Parables calls the heavenly judge "the Chosen One". The other reading, "the Son of God", fits the voice at the baptism in the other Gospels (Mark 1:11).

p: One of the two is Andrew (1:40). The other is never named. Many think he is the disciple Jesus loved.
b: John the Baptist had disciples of his own, who fasted and prayed (Mark 2:18; Luke 11:1). This Gospel says Jesus' first followers came from them. One is Andrew (1:40); the other is never named. Since the "disciple Jesus loved" is also never named and appears with Peter (13:23–24; 20:2), many readers since the early church have thought he is the second disciple here, which would make the Gospel's witness present from the first day. Others think the writer simply did not know or need the name.

p: Jesus' first words in John are a question every reader is asked. He asks it again at his arrest and at the tomb.
b: In this Gospel Jesus' first spoken words are "What are you looking for?" (ti zēteite). The same verb comes back at key moments: Jesus asks the soldiers who they are looking for (18:4, 7), and asks Mary Magdalene the same at the empty tomb (20:15). The disciples answer with their own question, "Where are you staying?", using menō (see 1:32). Many readers hear a deeper sense: they want to know where Jesus lives, and the Gospel will show that he dwells with the Father (14:2–3, 10).

p: Rabbi means "my great one", a respectful way to address a teacher. John translates it for his readers.
b: Rabbi is Hebrew and Aramaic for "my master" (from rav, "great"). In Jesus' day it was a polite way to address a respected teacher. Only after AD 70 did it become a formal title for ordained scholars. John explains it as "Teacher" (didaskalos), as he will explain "Messiah" and "Cephas" (1:41–42), which shows that his readers did not know Aramaic. Nicodemus and the disciples call Jesus "Rabbi" (3:2; 4:31); Mary Magdalene uses the longer form Rabbouni (20:16).

p: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the tenth hour was about 4 p.m. A few say John used Roman midnight time.
b: Jews, Greeks and Romans divided daylight into twelve hours counted from sunrise (compare 11:9), so the tenth hour is around 4 in the afternoon. That fits "they stayed... the rest of that day". A few writers, such as B. F. Westcott, argued that John counted from midnight, as Roman law courts did for legal days, which would make this 10 in the morning and change the times in 4:6 and 19:14. Most scholars think the evidence for a Roman "civil" reckoning of hours is weak. The precise time is the kind of detail an eyewitness would remember.

p: John keeps the Aramaic word in Greek letters, Messias, then translates it: Christ. It appears only here and in 4:25.
b: The Greek Messias spells the Aramaic meshicha, "anointed one". Only John in the New Testament keeps the Semitic word, here and on the Samaritan woman's lips (4:25), each time translating it as Christos. Elsewhere "Christ" is used as Jesus' name (1:17). The disciples' quick confession contrasts with the other Gospels, where Peter's confession comes much later (Mark 8:29). John may compress the story, or the disciples may have used the word before they understood it.

p: Kepha is Aramaic for "rock"; Petros is the Greek. Paul usually calls him Cephas.
b: Jesus gives Simon a new name, as God renamed Abram and Jacob. Kēphas spells the Aramaic kepha, "rock" or "stone"; Petros is a Greek form of the same word. Paul mostly calls him "Cephas" (1 Corinthians 1:12; 15:5; Galatians 2:9). In Matthew the naming comes after Peter's confession, with the words about building the church (Matthew 16:18); in John Jesus names him at their first meeting. Readers differ on what the name says about Peter's role in the church (see Matthew 16:18).
r: Matthew 16:17–18; Mark 3:16; Genesis 17:5; Genesis 32:28; 1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9; 21:15–19

p: To "follow" a teacher meant to become his disciple, walking behind him and learning his way of life.
b: Akoloutheō is the ordinary word for walking behind someone, but in the Gospels it means becoming a disciple. Students of teachers literally followed them from place to place. The two disciples "followed" Jesus (1:37), and now Jesus calls Philip in two words. The same call closes the Gospel, spoken to Peter: "Follow me" (21:19, 22). John's readers, who never saw Jesus, are invited to follow him too (8:12; 12:26).

p: A fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of Herod's son Philip.
b: Bethsaida ("house of fishing") lay where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee, just inside the territory of Philip the tetrarch, a son of Herod. Philip made it a city and named it Julias (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.28). Archaeologists debate whether the site is et-Tell or el-Araj, nearer the lake. Mark places Simon and Andrew's home in Capernaum (Mark 1:21, 29), so they may have grown up in Bethsaida and later moved. Philip and Andrew both have Greek names, perhaps a sign of a mixed area, and Greeks later approach Philip first (12:21).

p: His Hebrew name means "God has given." He is not in the lists of the Twelve, and he came from Cana.
b: Nathanael appears only in John, here and at the lake after the resurrection, where we learn he was "from Cana in Galilee" (21:2). He is not named in the Synoptic lists of the Twelve. From the 800s some writers identified him with Bartholomew, who is listed next to Philip (Mark 3:18), since Bartholomew is a family name ("son of Tolmai"). Others think he was a disciple outside the Twelve. His name (Hebrew Netan'el, "God has given") fits a Gospel that speaks of God's gifts (3:16; 4:10).

a: The one Moses wrote about in the law, and the prophets too
p: Philip does not say which passages. Early Christians pointed to Deuteronomy 18, Genesis 49 and many prophecies.
b: "The law and the prophets" was a common way to name the Scriptures. Philip may think of the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), the ruler from Judah (Genesis 49:10), or the son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Later Jesus himself says that Moses wrote about him (5:46). The phrase "Joseph's son" is how people knew Jesus (6:42); John's readers know from the prologue where he truly comes from.

a: Out of Nazareth, can anything good come?
p: Nazareth was a small farming village, never mentioned in the Old Testament. Nothing was expected from it.
b: Nazareth was a village of a few hundred people in the hills of lower Galilee, a few miles from the large Roman town of Sepphoris. It is never mentioned in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Mishnah. Nathanael's scorn may be simple village rivalry (he came from Cana, about eight miles away, 21:2), or the feeling that the Messiah could not come from a place the Scriptures never name (compare 7:41–42, 52). Philip does not argue. He answers with Jesus' own invitation: "Come and see" (1:39).

p: Jacob got his blessing by trickery and was renamed Israel. Nathanael is a true "Israel" without the trickery.
b: Isaac said of Jacob, "Your brother came with trickery and took your blessing" (Genesis 27:35), using the same word, dolos, in the Greek. Jacob was later renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28). Jesus calls Nathanael a true Israelite with no dolos, a Jacob without the trickery. The psalm also blesses the one "whose spirit holds no trickery" (Psalm 32:2). The Jacob theme continues in 1:51 with Jacob's dream of a stairway.
orig: ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν (en hō dolos ouk estin)

p: Sitting under one's own fig tree was a picture of peace. Jesus' knowledge of Nathanael is what amazes him.
b: The prophets pictured the coming age of peace as everyone sitting "under his vine and under his fig tree" (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10), and in Solomon's day Judah and Israel lived so (1 Kings 4:25). A fig tree gave shade for rest, prayer or study. The text does not say what Nathanael was doing. What matters is that Jesus saw him when no one else could, a knowledge of people that John stresses (2:24–25; 4:18).

a: you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel
t: Son of God, King of Israel
p: To a Jew of the time, both titles could name the coming king of David's line.
b: God promised David's son, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14), and in Psalm 2 the king set on Zion hears, "You are my son" (Psalm 2:7). So "Son of God" and "King of Israel" could both name the Messiah, and Nathanael probably means that. The crowd will hail Jesus as "King of Israel" (12:13), and Pilate will write "King of the Jews" over the cross (19:19). For John's readers "Son of God" means more, as the prologue has shown (1:14, 18).

a: Amen, amen, I tell you all
p: Others said "amen" to agree with someone else. Jesus says it first, doubled, to back his own words.
b: "Amen" is Hebrew for "surely, it is firm". People said it after a prayer or a curse to agree (Deuteronomy 27:15–26). Jesus puts it before his own sayings, which no one else is known to have done, and in John he always doubles it, twenty-five times. The KJV renders it "Verily, verily"; this site keeps "Amen, amen", as the Greek does. Here Jesus is speaking to Nathanael ("said to him"), but the "you" is plural: the promise is for all the disciples.
orig: Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν (Amēn amēn legō hymin)

a: God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man
p: Jacob saw "angels of God going up and going down on it." Jesus says they will do so on him.
b: At Bethel Jacob dreamed of "a stairway set up on the earth, its top reaching the sky, and look: angels of God going up and going down on it" (Genesis 28:12). The Hebrew bo can mean "on it" or "on him", and a rabbinic debate asks whether the angels went up and down on the stairway or on Jacob himself (Genesis Rabbah 68:12). Jesus claims to be the place where heaven and earth meet, the true Bethel ("house of God"). The next chapters develop this: Jesus' body is the temple (2:21).

p: Jesus' favorite title for himself. It recalls Daniel's "one like a son of man" who comes to God's throne.
b: In Hebrew and Aramaic "son of man" simply means "a human being" (Psalm 8:4). In Daniel's vision, "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting rule (Daniel 7:13–14). In the Gospels it is the title Jesus most often uses for himself, and almost no one else uses it of him. In John the Son of Man comes down from heaven and goes up again (3:13), is "lifted up" on the cross (3:14; 12:32–34), and is the judge (5:27).
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

p: Counted from 1:43, or a hint of Sinai and of Easter? John's days add up to a week.
b: "The third day" probably counts from Philip and Nathanael's call (1:43). Counting the days in chapter 1 (1:19, 29, 35, 43) and then "the third day" gives a week of seven days, and some readers see a new creation week that ends in a wedding. Others hear Sinai, where God showed his glory "on the third day" (Exodus 19:16), as Jesus shows his glory here (2:11). Christian readers also hear the resurrection on the third day. John does not explain, and the plain meaning is simply a time marker.

p: A village north of Nazareth. Most archaeologists place it at Khirbet Qana, not the tourist town of Kafr Kanna.
b: Cana is named only in John (2:1, 11; 4:46; 21:2). Josephus stayed at a village called Cana in Galilee (Life 86). Pilgrims today visit Kafr Kanna, about four miles north-east of Nazareth, but excavations at Khirbet Qana, about eight miles north of Nazareth, found a Jewish village of Jesus' time and a cave used by Christian pilgrims from the Byzantine period, and many scholars think this was the Cana of the Gospel. Nathanael came from there (21:2).

p: John never gives her name. She appears only here and at the cross, both times called "Woman."
b: This Gospel never names Mary, Jesus' mother; it calls her only "his mother" (2:1–12; 6:42; 19:25–27). She appears at the beginning of Jesus' signs and at the cross, and both times he addresses her as "Woman". Many readers see the two scenes as a pair: here his "hour" has not come (2:4); at the cross it has, and he gives her to the disciple he loved (19:26–27). Catholic and Orthodox readers have seen in her a figure of the church, or a new Eve ("woman", Genesis 3:15).

p: A village wedding lasted days. Running out of wine shamed the groom's family before the whole town.
b: Jewish weddings were the great feasts of village life and could last a week (compare Judges 14:12; Tobit 11:19). The groom's family hosted, and guests often brought gifts, so running short was a public embarrassment, and possibly a debt of honor. Mary's words state the need without asking for anything directly, the way a polite request was often made. Why she turns to Jesus the story does not say; perhaps she was helping the family, and perhaps she already expected something of him.

p: It sounds harsh in English, but Jesus uses it kindly for other women. It is strange from a son to a mother.
b: Gynai, "woman", was a polite form of address. Jesus uses it for the Samaritan woman (4:21), for Mary Magdalene at the tomb (20:15) and for his mother from the cross, in a moment of great care (19:26). So the word is not rude, as "Woman!" might sound in English. But no other ancient text shows a son calling his mother "woman", so it does set a distance: in his work Jesus answers to his Father, not to family wishes (compare Mark 3:31–35). Some translations soften it as "Dear woman".

a: What does that have to do with me and you
p: A Hebrew idiom found across the Bible. It usually pushes back: "That is not our concern" or "Why involve me?"
b: The Greek copies a Hebrew idiom, literally "what to me and to you?" Jephthah says it to the Ammonite king, "What is there between you and me?" (Judges 11:12), and the widow says it to Elijah (1 Kings 17:18); demons say it to Jesus (Mark 1:24). It always marks some distance, from mild ("that is not our business") to hostile. Here it is mild, since Mary is not offended and tells the servants to obey him. Catholic readers stress that Jesus still acts at her word; many Protestant readers stress the distance.
orig: Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (Ti emoi kai soi)

a: My hour is not here yet
p: Jesus' "hour" is the time of his death and glory. Until 12:23 it has "not yet come."
b: Throughout the first half of the Gospel Jesus' "hour" has not yet come (7:30; 8:20), and enemies cannot seize him. Then, when Greeks ask to see him, he says that the hour is here for the Son of Man to be glorified (12:23), and the passion begins (13:1; 17:1). So already at Cana the wine points ahead to the cross. Some readers also take "my hour" here more simply: the time for Jesus to show himself publicly.

a: Whatever he says to you, do it.
p: Mary's words echo Pharaoh's in a famine: "Go to Joseph. Do whatever he tells you."
b: When Egypt was starving, "Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, 'Go to Joseph. Do whatever he tells you'" (Genesis 41:55), and Joseph opened the storehouses. Mary's words to the servants echo this: she points away from herself to the one who can supply what is lacking. They are her last words in this Gospel. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often cite them in their devotion to Mary, while Protestants often cite them as a model of pointing to Christ alone; the two need not conflict (see the card below).

p: Stone, unlike clay, could not become ritually impure. Archaeologists find stone vessels all over Judea and Galilee.
b: Under the purity rules later collected in the Mishnah, a clay pot that became impure had to be broken, but stone vessels could not become impure at all (Mishnah Kelim 10:1; Parah 3:2). So in Jesus' time Jews in Judea and Galilee made and used stone cups, bowls and large jars, found at many sites. Yitzhak Magen studied the workshops near Jerusalem; quarries and workshops in Galilee, at Reina near Nazareth and Einot Amitai near Cana, were excavated by others (Shimon Gibson, Yonatan Adler). The water was for washing hands and vessels before meals (Mark 7:3–4). John explains it for readers who did not know the custom. Some see meaning in the number six, one short of a perfect seven, but John does not say so.

p: A measure (metrētēs) was about 39 liters, so the jars held some 120 to 180 gallons in all.
b: The metrētēs was a liquid measure of about 39 liters, roughly 10 gallons. Six jars of two or three measures each held some 450 to 700 liters, about 120 to 180 gallons: far more than any village wedding could drink. The prophets pictured the coming age with wine in abundance: "the mountains will drip with sweet wine" (Amos 9:13), and a Jewish apocalypse of about AD 100 imagines vines with a thousand branches (2 Baruch 29:5). The overflow of good wine is a sign that the time of the Messiah's feast has begun.

a: the man in charge of the feast
p: Greek architriklinos: the guest or servant in charge of the banquet, who tasted the wine and ran the tables.
b: The architriklinos (literally "ruler of the three-couch dining room") was the person in charge of a banquet: sometimes a head servant, sometimes a guest chosen to preside, who managed the food and drink and proposed toasts. Sirach advises such a person to look after the guests first (Sirach 35:1–2). He does not know where the wine came from, but the servants do: in John, those who serve and obey know what the important people miss.

a: tasted the water, now turned into wine
p: Greeks told of the wine god Dionysus filling empty jars with wine. Most scholars doubt that John borrowed from it.
b: The Greek god Dionysus was the giver of wine. Pausanias, writing in the 100s AD, reports that at Elis priests set three empty basins in a sealed building during the festival of Dionysus and found them full of wine the next day (Description of Greece 6.26.1–2), and similar wonders were told of other shrines. Rudolf Bultmann argued that the Cana story was modeled on such tales, to show Jesus outdoing Dionysus. Martin Hengel and most later scholars answer that the story is thoroughly Jewish: stone jars for purity water, a village wedding, and the prophets' hope of abundant wine in the age to come. Readers who knew Dionysus might still have noticed the contrast, but direct borrowing is unlikely.

p: The verb means "get drunk." The steward is describing a common practice, not saying this crowd was drunk.
b: Methysthōsin means "they have become drunk". Some translators soften it to "have drunk freely", but the word means drunkenness elsewhere (Luke 12:45; 1 Thessalonians 5:7). The steward is quoting a general practice, half joking: hosts serve the cheap wine when people can no longer tell. Some Christians who teach total abstinence have argued that the wine at Cana was unfermented juice; Ellen G. White, a founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, taught this (The Desire of Ages, chapter 15). Most scholars, including many who practice abstinence, think it was ordinary wine; the steward's joke assumes it. See the card below.

a: You have kept the good wine until now
p: Readers have heard the old order giving way to the new, and God saving his best for the end.
b: The steward's words carry more meaning than he knows. Many readers take the best wine "until now" as the new gift Jesus brings, better than what went before, poured out from jars used for Jewish purity washings. Read so, the story is not a judgment on Judaism but a claim that the hoped-for messianic time has arrived, a theme the prophets used for the joy of the end (Isaiah 25:6). In the other Gospels Jesus speaks of new wine in new wineskins (Mark 2:22).

p: John does not say "miracles" or "mighty works." He calls them signs: deeds that point beyond themselves.
b: The other Gospels call Jesus' miracles dynameis, "powerful deeds". John calls them sēmeia, "signs", acts that point to who Jesus is and lead to faith (20:30–31). He numbers the first two (2:11; 4:54). Most readers count seven before the cross: water into wine, the official's son, the man at Bethesda, the feeding, walking on the sea, the man born blind, and Lazarus. Many scholars (Bultmann, Fortna) think John drew on an earlier written "signs source" that numbered them. "Beginning" (archē) may also mean "first in importance", the sign that shows what the rest mean.

p: John mentions Jesus' brothers here and in 7:3–10. Who they were is debated among churches.
b: The brothers appear again in 7:3–5, where they do not yet believe in him. Christians have understood "brothers" in three ways: younger sons of Mary and Joseph (most Protestants, following Helvidius in the 300s); sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Orthodox, following the Protevangelium of James and Epiphanius); or cousins (Catholic, following Jerome). Greek adelphos normally means brother, but in the Greek Old Testament it can stand for a wider relative, since Hebrew has no separate word for cousin (Genesis 13:8, of Abram and Lot).

p: A fishing town on the north shore of the lake, Jesus' base in the other Gospels. John mentions it only briefly.
b: Capernaum (Kefar Nahum, "Nahum's village") lay on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee. The other Gospels make it Jesus' home base (Mark 2:1). Visitors today see a fine white limestone synagogue built in the 300s or 400s on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and a house venerated from early times as Peter's. In John it is where Jesus later gives the bread of life speech (6:59). One goes "down" to Capernaum because it lies far below the hills of Cana and Nazareth, near the lake, about 700 feet below sea level.

p: John names three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), so Jesus' ministry lasts two or three years, not one.
b: In Mark, Jesus goes to Jerusalem only once, at the end, so his ministry could fit in a year. John names three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), another unnamed festival (5:1), Booths (7:2) and Dedication (10:22), and Jesus goes up to Jerusalem often, as devout Jews did. This is the main source of the traditional picture of a ministry of about three years. Many historians think John's frequent visits to Jerusalem are likely, since Jesus was known there at his arrest. Saying "the Jews' Passover" helps readers outside Judaism; it does not mean Jesus stood outside it.

t: Animals and money in the temple
p: Pilgrims needed approved animals for sacrifice and Tyrian silver for the temple tax. Trade was needed, but where?
b: Worshipers coming from far away bought animals for sacrifice in Jerusalem rather than drive them for days, and each adult Jewish man paid a yearly half-shekel temple tax (Exodus 30:13) in a coin of high silver content, the shekel of Tyre (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3; Babylonian Talmud Bekhorot 50b). Money changers set up their tables in the temple area before Passover. The trade itself served worship. What is debated is whether it had moved into the temple's outer court, the only part open to non-Jews, and whether Jesus objected to commerce, to dishonest dealing, or to the temple system itself.

p: Only John mentions a whip. Did Jesus use it on people or only on the animals?
b: The other Gospels say Jesus drove out the sellers and overturned tables (Mark 11:15). Only John mentions a whip of cords, probably made from rush or rope lying at hand, since weapons were not allowed in the temple. The Greek "all" (pantas, masculine) is then explained by "both the sheep and the cattle", so many readers, especially in the peace churches (Mennonites and other Anabaptists), conclude that the whip drove the animals, not the people. Others take it as a show of force aimed at the traders too. The passage has been cited both for and against Christian use of force.

a: Stop turning my Father's house into a house for trading!
p: Jesus calls the temple "my Father's house." The prophet Zechariah promised a day with no traders in God's house.
b: In the other Gospels Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 about a "house of prayer" turned into a "cave for bandits" (Matthew 21:13). In John he speaks in his own voice, as a son: "my Father's house", as the boy Jesus did in Luke 2:49. The phrase "house for trading" (literally "house of trade") may echo Zechariah's final vision, when every pot in Jerusalem will be holy and "there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD" on that day (Zechariah 14:21). The act is a prophetic sign that the end-time purity of God's house is near.
r: Zechariah 14:21; Luke 2:49; 14:2; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Matthew 21:13; Malachi 3:1–3

a: Zeal for your house will eat me up.
p: The psalm says "has eaten me up"; John's Greek says "will eat me up," a hint that zeal will cost Jesus his life.
b: The disciples recall Psalm 69:9, which this site renders, "Zeal for your house has eaten me up" (Psalm 69:9). The Hebrew and the Septuagint have a past tense; John's quotation has a future, "will eat me up", which points to Jesus' death: his zeal for God's house will consume him. Psalm 69, a lament of a righteous sufferer, is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament: its "vinegar" returns at the cross (19:28–29; Psalm 69:21), and Paul quotes the second half of verse 9 of Christ (Romans 15:3).

p: Mark, Matthew and Luke put the temple scene in Jesus' last week; John puts it at the start. Was it once or twice?
b: In the Synoptic Gospels the clearing of the temple happens after the entry into Jerusalem and leads to Jesus' arrest (Mark 11:15–18). John places it at the first Passover. Readers explain this in three ways. (1) Two events: Jesus did it twice, near the start and near the end (many traditional harmonies, D. A. Carson). (2) John moved it to the front, like an overture, to show from the start that Jesus replaces the temple (most critical scholars). (3) John is right and the Synoptics compressed everything into one visit (J. A. T. Robinson). The saying itself was quoted against Jesus at his trial in a twisted form (Mark 14:58), and the Greek here is an ironic command: "You go ahead and destroy it."
orig: Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον (Lysate ton naon touton)

a: Forty-six years this temple was under construction
p: Herod began rebuilding the temple about 20 BC. Forty-six years later points to about AD 27 or 28.
b: Josephus says Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20–19 BC (Jewish Antiquities 15.380). Counting forty-six years gives about AD 27–28 for this Passover, which fits Luke's date for John's preaching, the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1). The sanctuary itself was finished quickly, but work on the courts went on until about AD 63, only seven years before the Romans destroyed it all. The Greek can also mean "this sanctuary was built forty-six years ago."

a: the temple he meant was the temple of his body
p: John explains the riddle: the temple Jesus would raise was his own body. God's presence now lives in a person.
b: The narrator steps in to explain. In the Bible the temple was the place where God's name and glory lived among his people. John has said the Word "pitched his tent among us" (1:14), and Jesus said that angels would go up and down on him like Jacob's "house of God" (1:51). Now Jesus' body is the true temple, destroyed and raised in three days. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that worship will no longer be tied to a mountain or to Jerusalem (4:21–24), and Revelation's new Jerusalem has no temple, "because the Lord God, the Almighty, is its temple, and so is the Lamb" (Revelation 21:22). The church later called itself God's temple too (1 Corinthians 3:16).

a: his disciples remembered he used to say this
p: John admits the disciples understood only after Easter. The Spirit would remind them (14:26).
b: John says openly that the disciples did not understand at the time; after the resurrection they "remembered" and believed both the Scripture and Jesus' word. He says the same of the entry into Jerusalem (12:16), and Jesus promises that the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, will remind them of everything he said (14:26). Some scholars take this as a sign that the Gospel is shaped by later reflection; others see an honest witness telling what he understood then and what he understood later. Both may be true.

a: Jesus, for his part, did not trust himself to them
p: The same verb twice: many "believed" in him, but he did not "entrust" himself to them.
b: John plays on pisteuō: many episteusan ("believed") in his name, but Jesus ouk episteuen himself to them ("did not entrust"). A faith that rests only on seeing wonders is not yet the trust John wants (4:48; 6:26; 20:29). Jesus knew "what was inside a man" (2:25), as God alone knows hearts (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The next verse begins, "One of the Pharisees was a man": the story of one such man, Nicodemus, who came because of the signs (3:2).
orig: οὐκ ἐπίστευεν αὑτὸν αὐτοῖς (ouk episteuen hauton autois)

p: A Pharisee and a member of the ruling council. He appears three times in John, each time a little bolder.
b: Nicodemus has a Greek name ("victor over the people"), common among Jews of the time. "A leader of the Jews" probably means he sat on the Jerusalem council, the Sanhedrin (7:50). He comes by night here, defends Jesus' right to a hearing in 7:50–51, and brings a huge amount of spices to bury him in 19:39. The Talmud tells of a wealthy Jerusalemite named Naqdimon ben Gurion in the years before AD 70 (Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 19b–20a; Gittin 56a); whether he is the same man is unknown. Readers still debate whether Nicodemus became a believer.

p: Night may show fear of being seen, or the time for study. In John, night also means the darkness of unbelief.
b: Readers give three reasons Nicodemus came at night. He feared being seen with Jesus, as other leaders did (12:42); 19:39 recalls that he "had come to Jesus by night". Or night was a quiet time for teachers to study and talk, as rabbis later praised studying the Torah at night. Or John uses night as a symbol: he comes out of darkness toward the light (3:19–21), while Judas goes out from the light "and it was night" (13:30). The three need not exclude each other.

t: Born again, or born from above?
p: Anōthen means both "from above" and "again." Jesus means from above; Nicodemus hears "again."
b: The adverb anōthen can mean "from above" (as in 3:31 and 19:11, 23) or "again, anew" (Galatians 4:9). Nicodemus takes it the second way and asks about entering his mother's womb "a second time" (3:4). In John's usage the main sense is "from above": a birth from God (1:13), by the Spirit (3:5–8). Many scholars think John meant both, and that Nicodemus' mistake is a deliberate misunderstanding that lets Jesus explain. The KJV and most English Bibles say "born again"; this translation says "from above", with "again" in the gloss.

p: The other Gospels' great theme appears in John only here and in 3:5. Elsewhere John speaks of eternal life.
b: "The kingdom of God" (basileia, also "reign") is the center of Jesus' preaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke: God ruling as king, now and at the end. John uses the phrase only in this conversation (3:3, 5); elsewhere he speaks of "eternal life", which he introduces a few verses later (3:15–16). Many scholars think John translated the kingdom message into the language of life for his readers. Jesus will later tell Pilate that his kingdom does not come from this world (18:36).
orig: τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ (tēn basileian tou theou)

p: Nicodemus takes Jesus literally. John often lets people misunderstand so that Jesus can explain the deeper meaning.
b: Again and again in John, people take Jesus' words on the wrong level: the temple (2:20–21), birth (3:4), water (4:11–15), food (4:33), bread (6:34, 52), going away (7:35; 8:22), sleep (11:12–13). The misunderstanding gives Jesus a chance to explain, and lets the reader see more than the person in the story. Nicodemus is not foolish: his question shows that human effort cannot produce a new birth, which is Jesus' point.

p: Baptism? Natural birth? The Spirit's cleansing promised in Ezekiel? This is one of the most debated phrases in John.
b: The Greek joins "water and Spirit" under one preposition, as one birth. Readers have taken "water" as: (1) Christian baptism, the reading of nearly all early Christian writers (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian) and of Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching; (2) the Spirit's cleansing, with water as a picture of what the Spirit does, as in Ezekiel's promise of clean water, a new heart and God's Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27), a view of Calvin and many Reformed and Baptist interpreters; (3) natural birth, the water of the womb, followed by spiritual birth (3:6); (4) John's baptism of repentance, which Nicodemus could understand. Nicodemus was rebuked for not knowing this (3:10), which favors an Old Testament background. See the card below.

a: What is born from the flesh is flesh
p: Here "flesh" is not sinful but simply human. Human life can only produce human life.
b: In this Gospel "flesh" means human nature in its weakness, not sin as such: the Word himself "became flesh" (1:14). The point is about origins: like produces like. Human birth produces human beings; only God's Spirit can produce spiritual life. Jesus will say the same about his words: it is the Spirit that gives life, and the flesh does not help (6:63). Paul's use of "flesh" for human nature set against God (Romans 8:5–8) is related but not the same.

a: You people must be born from above
p: Jesus turns from "you" singular to "you" plural. He speaks past Nicodemus to the group he represents.
b: Up to here Jesus has said "you" (singular) to Nicodemus. Now he says "you all" (hymas), and in 3:11–12 the plural continues: "you people do not receive what we testify." Nicodemus had begun, "we know" (3:2), speaking for others. Jesus answers the group: the teachers of Israel, and every reader, need this birth. English "you" hides the shift, so this translation writes "you people".

a: The wind blows where it wants to
p: In Greek, as in Hebrew, the same word means "wind" and "spirit." Jesus plays on it.
b: Pneuma, like Hebrew ruach, means wind, breath and spirit. "The sound of it" (phōnē) can also mean "voice". So the verse can be read on two levels at once: the wind blows where it wants and you hear its sound, and the Spirit moves where he wills and you hear his voice. You cannot see the wind or control it, but you can see its effects. Ezekiel's vision of dry bones has the same play: the breath, the winds and the Spirit bring the dead to life (Ezekiel 37:9–14).
orig: τὸ πνεῦμα ὅπου θέλει πνεῖ (to pneuma hopou thelei pnei)

p: The article ("the teacher") suggests Nicodemus was a well-known teacher. There is irony in the question.
b: Jesus says "the" teacher, not "a" teacher, as if Nicodemus were the recognized teacher of the nation, or as a gentle mockery. Nicodemus opened by calling Jesus a teacher come from God (3:2); now the roles are reversed. The things he should have known are in the Scriptures he taught: God's promise of a new heart and his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27), and of a people renewed by his breath (Ezekiel 37).

p: Jesus suddenly says "we." Is it Jesus with John the Baptist, with his disciples, or the church speaking?
b: The plural is surprising. Some think Jesus includes John the Baptist and the prophets, who also testified. Some think he speaks with his disciples, answering Nicodemus' "we know" (3:2) with a "we" of his own. Many scholars hear the voice of the later church in debate with the synagogue: "we" believers testify, "you" do not receive it. Others note that Jesus may be using a plural of authority. The same contrast between "we" and "you" appears in 1 John 1:1–3.

a: nobody has gone up into heaven
t: Who has gone up to heaven?
p: Jewish writings told of Moses, Enoch and Elijah going up to heaven. Jesus says only the one who came down has.
b: Proverbs asks, "Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down?" (Proverbs 30:4), and Deuteronomy says God's command is not in the sky, so no one need climb up for it (Deuteronomy 30:12). Jewish writings of the time told of Enoch, Moses and others going up to heaven to receive revelation (1 Enoch 14; 70–71). Jesus claims that no one has gone up to bring back heavenly knowledge except the Son of Man, who came down from heaven in the first place. Paul uses Deuteronomy 30:12 of Christ too (Romans 10:6–7).

a: Moses raised the snake high in the wilderness
p: Bitten Israelites looked at a bronze snake on a pole and lived. Jesus compares it to his own lifting up.
b: When snakes bit the people in the wilderness, the LORD told Moses, "Make yourself a burning one and put it on a pole. Anyone who has been bitten and looks at it will live" (Numbers 21:8). Jewish readers took care to say that the snake itself did not heal. The Wisdom of Solomon calls it "a symbol of salvation" (Wisdom of Solomon 16:6–7), and the Mishnah asks, "Could the snake kill or give life?" and answers that Israel lived when they looked up and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Jesus' comparison is about looking in trust at the one lifted up on a pole, the cross.

p: Hypsoō means both "raise high" and "exalt." In John the cross is where Jesus is lifted up and glorified.
b: Hypsoō means to raise something high, and also to exalt or honor someone. Isaiah's servant "will be high and lifted up" (Isaiah 52:13), in the Greek with the same verb. John uses it three times of Jesus (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–34), and in 12:33 he explains that it pointed to the kind of death Jesus would die. For John the crucifixion is not a defeat followed by glory; it is itself the lifting up. "Has to" (dei) speaks of God's plan.

p: Literally "life of the age": the life of the world to come, which John says begins now for those who believe.
b: Zōē aiōnios is literally "life of the age". Jews spoke of "this age" and "the age to come", and "life of the age" was the life of the coming age, given at the resurrection (Daniel 12:2, the only place the phrase appears in the Hebrew Bible). John uses the phrase seventeen times and stresses that the believer "has" it now (3:36; 5:24), while still awaiting the resurrection (6:40). It is more a quality of life, knowing God (17:3), than mere endless length.

a: this is how God loved the world
p: Many hear "God so loved" as "God loved so much." The Greek houtōs means "in this way": by giving his Son.
b: Houtōs normally means "thus, in this way", pointing to how something was done, as in 3:14, "so the Son of Man has to be lifted up". The KJV's "God so loved the world" is often heard as "God loved the world so much". That is true, but the Greek stresses the manner of God's love: this is the way he loved, by giving. The verb is an aorist ("loved"), pointing to the act of giving the Son, above all on the cross. In 1611 the KJV's "so" could itself mean "in this way", and some grammarians think houtōs ... hōste also carries a sense of degree ("so much that"), so both ideas may be present. The other Gospels never say that God loved "the world" in these words.
orig: Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον

a: For this is how God loved the world:
p: Ancient Greek had no quotation marks. Does Jesus' speech end at 3:15, or run to 3:21?
b: Greek manuscripts had no quotation marks, so translators must decide where Jesus stops speaking. Many scholars think the words from 3:16 on are John's own reflection: they speak of Jesus in the past tense ("he gave", "light has entered the world"), and of the "only Son", a phrase Jesus never uses of himself elsewhere. Others, and most red-letter Bibles, keep 3:16–21 in Jesus' mouth. In John the voices of Jesus and the narrator often blend. This translation follows most English Bibles in closing the quotation at 3:21, and it does not open a fresh quotation mark at 3:16, so the verse reads as Jesus' words continuing. The same question arises in 3:31–36.

p: "Only Son" recalls Isaac, whom Abraham did not withhold. Paul draws the same line in Romans 8:32.
b: God told Abraham, "Take your son, please, your only one, whom you love, Isaac" (Genesis 22:2). Jewish tradition called the story the Akedah, "the binding", and saw great merit in Abraham's willingness. Many readers hear it behind God's giving of his only Son, as Paul does: God "did not hold back his own Son" (Romans 8:32), with words that echo the Greek of Genesis 22:16. For "only" (monogenēs), see 1:14. "Gave" covers both the sending into the world (3:17) and the giving up to death.

p: Apollymi means to be lost, ruined or destroyed. What "perishing" is has been read in more than one way.
b: Apolētai is used of a lost sheep and the lost son (Luke 15:4, 24), of food that spoils (6:27) and of people destroyed (10:10). Here it is the opposite of eternal life. Most churches have taught that it means lasting separation from God under judgment (3:36; 5:29). Some Christians ("conditional immortality", taught for example by Seventh-day Adventists and by some Anglican and evangelical scholars) take it to mean that the unsaved finally cease to exist. A few hold that God will in the end save all. The verse itself stresses God's purpose: that people not perish.

a: to pass judgment on the world
p: Krinō means to judge, and often to condemn. Jesus did not come for that, yet his coming brings a verdict.
b: Krinō means to decide, judge, and often to condemn. Many translations say "condemn" here. John holds two sides together: the Son was not sent to condemn (3:17; 12:47), yet the Father has given him all judgment (5:22, 27), and he says he came into the world for judgment (9:39). The answer in 3:18–19 is that the verdict is already being given as people respond to the light. The world is not the enemy God wants to destroy, but the object of his saving purpose.

p: In John the last judgment is partly already here: people's response to Jesus is the verdict.
b: Jewish hope looked for a final judgment at the end of the age, and John keeps that hope (5:28–29; 12:48). But he stresses that the verdict is already given now: whoever believes "is not judged"; whoever does not believe "has been judged already" (the Greek perfect, a settled state). Scholars call this "realized eschatology" (C. H. Dodd's term), the end times already present. Most now speak of an "already and not yet": eternal life and judgment begin now and are completed at the last day.

a: the one who practices the truth
p: "To do the truth" is a Hebrew way of speaking: to live faithfully. The Dead Sea Scrolls use the same phrase.
b: In Greek, truth is something you know; in Hebrew thought, truth (emet) is faithfulness, something you do. "To do truth" appears in the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 47:29, of keeping faith) and in the Dead Sea Scrolls, where members pledge "to practice truth, righteousness and justice" (Community Rule, 1QS 1:5). Its opposite here is "doing wicked things" (3:20). People who live honestly before God are not afraid of being seen; they come to the light.
orig: ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν (ho poiōn tēn alētheian)

p: Only John says Jesus baptized. 4:2 adds that his disciples did it. Historians weigh both statements.
b: The other Gospels never mention Jesus baptizing during his ministry. John says so here and in 4:1, then adds that "Jesus himself was not baptizing; his disciples were" (4:2). Many historians think the first statement is old and likely: Jesus began as a follower of John and carried on his practice for a while. The correction in 4:2 may come from an editor who wanted to keep Jesus distinct from John, or may simply clarify. After the resurrection, baptism becomes the church's practice (Matthew 28:19).

p: Aenon means "springs." Its location is uncertain: in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria near Shechem.
b: Ainōn comes from Aramaic for "springs", which fits "many waters". Eusebius placed Aenon eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean) in the Jordan valley (Onomasticon), where pilgrims later visited it. Others point to a Salim east of Shechem in Samaria, near the springs of the Wadi Far'ah; if so, John was baptizing in Samaria, which would prepare for chapter 4. The detail is the kind of local knowledge that makes many historians respect John's topography.

a: before John was thrown into prison
p: John explains to readers who know Mark that Jesus' work began before the Baptist's arrest.
b: Mark says Jesus began preaching in Galilee "after John was arrested" (Mark 1:14). John's narrator steps in to say that this scene came earlier, while both men were baptizing. The remark assumes readers already know of John's imprisonment, which this Gospel never narrates. Richard Bauckham and others take this as a sign that John wrote for readers who knew Mark's Gospel; others think the story was simply well known.

p: In a Jewish wedding the groom's friend helped arrange it and waited to hear the groom's voice with joy.
b: At Jewish weddings a close friend of the groom (later called the shoshbin) helped negotiate and arrange the marriage and brought the bride to the groom. His joy was complete when he heard the groom's voice with the bride. The prophets pictured God as Israel's husband: "With a bridegroom's joy over his bride your God will rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5; compare Hosea 2:19–20). John casts Jesus as the groom and himself as the friend, so he rejoices, not envies, that the crowds go to Jesus. The other Gospels also call Jesus the groom (Mark 2:19–20).
r: Isaiah 54:5; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20; Mark 2:19–20; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 19:7; Revelation 21:2

a: He must keep growing, and I must keep getting smaller
p: The last words of John the Baptist in this Gospel. The church sets his birth near the longest day, Jesus' near the shortest.
b: These are John's last recorded words in this Gospel, and they sum up his role: he points away from himself. The church came to celebrate John's birth on June 24, near the summer solstice, after which the days grow shorter, and Jesus' birth on December 25, near the winter solstice, after which they grow longer. Augustine, in his tractates on John, noted that John grew smaller by being beheaded while Christ grew by being lifted up on the cross, and his sermons for John's feast (Sermons 287 and 380) linked the verse to the shortening and lengthening days. The dates come from Luke's six-month gap between the two births (Luke 1:36), not from this verse, but preachers have linked them ever since.

a: The one coming from above stands over everyone
p: These verses may continue John the Baptist's words, or they may be the Gospel writer's comment.
b: There are no quotation marks in Greek. 3:31–36 can be read as the Baptist's continued testimony, or as the narrator's reflection, like 3:16–21, which they closely resemble: "from above", testimony not received, eternal life, the Father's love for the Son. Many modern translations end the Baptist's words at 3:30. This translation does too, but readers have long taken them both ways. Metzger reports that some witnesses, among them Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus' first hand and Bezae, lack the second "stands over everyone", which NA28 prints in brackets.

p: A seal pressed into wax or clay certified a document. Believing God's witness is like signing that God is true.
b: In the ancient world a person confirmed a document by pressing his seal into clay or wax (Jeremiah 32:10). To accept Jesus' testimony is to put one's seal on it: to certify that God tells the truth. In 6:27 God himself puts his seal on the Son. The opposite is in 1 John 5:10: whoever does not believe God has made him a liar.

p: A rabbinic saying held that the prophets received the Spirit "by measure." The Son has it in full.
b: A later rabbinic teaching says the holy spirit rested on the prophets "by measure", each having a certain amount (Leviticus Rabbah 15:2). Against that background John says the Spirit is given without measure. It is debated who gives and who receives: God gives the Spirit to the Son without limit (most readers, and the Byzantine text, which adds "God"), or the Son gives the Spirit without limit to believers. The first fits 1:32–33 and 3:35; the second fits 7:39 and 20:22.
orig: οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν τὸ πνεῦμα

p: The only mention of God's wrath in John. It "stays" on the one who refuses the Son, the same verb used for the Spirit.
b: Orgē, God's settled anger against evil, appears only here in John. It "stays" (menei) on the one who will not obey the Son, the same verb used for the Spirit staying on Jesus (1:32). The verse sets "believe" against "refuse to obey" (apeitheō): in John, believing is not only agreeing but submitting. The present tense "stays" suggests wrath is not newly imposed but remains where nothing has taken it away (compare 1:29).
orig: ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ μένει ἐπ’ αὐτόν

a: (To be exact, Jesus himself was not baptizing; his disciples were.)
p: This aside corrects 3:22 and 4:1. Many scholars think a later editor added it.
b: The narrator has twice said that Jesus was baptizing (3:22; 4:1). Now he qualifies it: the disciples did the baptizing. Some scholars see the hand of a final editor who wanted to avoid making Jesus look like a follower of John the Baptist. Others think it simply clarifies: Jesus' disciples baptized under his authority, the way a teacher "does" what his students do for him. Either way, the Gospel never shows Jesus baptizing anyone in a scene.

a: His road had to take him through Samaria
p: The shortest road from Judea to Galilee ran through Samaria. "Had to" may also hint at God's plan.
b: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Josephus says Galileans going to festivals in Jerusalem usually traveled through Samaria (Antiquities 20.118), the quickest route, about three days (Life 269), though some pious Jews took the longer way down the Jordan valley to avoid Samaritans. "Had to" (edei) is the same word used for God's purpose in 3:14 and 3:30, so many readers hear more than geography: Jesus had to go because of the meeting ahead.
orig: ἔδει δὲ αὐτὸν διέρχεσθαι (edei de auton dierchesthai)

p: Sychar was probably the village of Askar, near ancient Shechem, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
b: Sychar is named nowhere else. Most scholars identify it with the village of Askar, about a kilometer north-east of Jacob's well, on the slope of Mount Ebal. Some early copies of the Syriac read "Shechem", and Jerome thought the name was a corruption of it. Shechem itself, nearby at Tell Balata, was the place where Abraham first built an altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7) and where Joshua renewed the covenant (Joshua 24). Shechem was the Samaritans' center, under Mount Gerizim.

a: the field Jacob gave to Joseph his son
p: Jacob bought land at Shechem, gave Joseph an extra share, and Joseph was buried there.
b: Jacob bought "the piece of land where he had pitched his tent" near Shechem (Genesis 33:19). On his deathbed he gave Joseph "one shoulder of land" above his brothers (Genesis 48:22): the Hebrew word for "shoulder" is shechem, a pun on the town's name. Joseph's bones were buried there, "in the plot of ground Jacob had bought" (Joshua 24:32). Joseph's tomb is still shown near Nablus. Samaritans claimed descent from Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh.
