p: Genesis never mentions it, but the well is still there, over 100 feet deep, under a church at Nablus.
b: The Old Testament does not mention a well dug by Jacob, but local tradition claimed one. A well about 40 meters (some 130 feet) deep when cleared, less when choked with debris, at the foot of Mount Gerizim, has been shown as Jacob's well since at least the 300s, when the Bordeaux Pilgrim (AD 333) and Eusebius mention it; a church was built over it, and an Orthodox church stands there today. John calls it both a "spring" (pēgē, 4:6, 14) and a "well" (phrear, 4:11–12): it was fed by groundwater, so both are true, and Jesus plays on the difference.

p: The sixth hour after sunrise is about noon. Many readers say the woman came then to avoid others; that may read too much in.
b: Counting from sunrise, the sixth hour is about noon, the hottest part of the day. Many preachers say the woman came then to avoid the other women, who drew water in the cool of morning or evening, because she was an outcast. The text does not say so, and some scholars caution against the idea. Others note that the sixth hour is also the hour of Jesus' condemnation (19:14), when once again he thirsts (19:28).

a: a woman of Samaria arrived to draw water
p: In the Bible a man meeting a woman at a well often leads to a marriage: Isaac, Jacob and Moses.
b: Abraham's servant found Rebekah for Isaac at a well (Genesis 24). Jacob met Rachel at a well and rolled the stone off its mouth (Genesis 29:10). Moses ran from Pharaoh, "sat down by the well" and met his future wife (Exodus 2:15–21). John has just called Jesus the groom (3:29). Readers who knew these stories would expect a betrothal. Instead the scene turns to true worship, and the woman brings her town to Jesus. Many see a picture of Jesus gathering a people as a groom gathers a bride.

a: (For Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans.)
p: The verb may mean "do not share vessels with," not "have no dealings with." Jesus' disciples had gone to buy food from Samaritans.
b: Synchraomai can mean "to have dealings with" or, more strictly, "to use together". David Daube argued that it means Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans, since a Jewish ruling later written down in the Mishnah treated Samaritan women as always ritually unclean (Mishnah Niddah 4:1). This translation follows his reading. That explains why Jesus' request is surprising: he would drink from her jar. The broader sense cannot be right, since the disciples were buying food in a Samaritan town (4:8). Some manuscripts lack this aside; see the variant.

a: I am a woman of Samaria
p: They worshiped Israel's God, kept the five books of Moses and had their own temple on Mount Gerizim.
b: The Samaritans lived in the old northern heartland of Israel. Jews said they descended from foreigners settled there by Assyria, who "feared the LORD and served their carved images too" (2 Kings 17:41). Samaritans said, and still say, that they are the true descendants of Israel's northern tribes. They kept the five books of Moses in their own edition and worshiped on Mount Gerizim. Excavations there found a sacred precinct from the mid-400s BC; Josephus places the building of the temple in Alexander the Great's time (Antiquities 11.310–324). The Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed it, about 128 BC by Josephus' account (Antiquities 13.255–256) or about 111 BC by the coin evidence. A small Samaritan community still lives on Mount Gerizim today.

p: To the woman, "living water" means fresh running water. Jesus means the life God gives, which 7:39 calls the Spirit.
b: In ordinary speech "living water" meant running water from a spring or stream, better than water standing in a cistern. The woman hears it that way (4:11). But the prophets called God "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13), and Zechariah saw living water flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). In 7:37–39 John explains that Jesus' "living water" is the Spirit that believers would receive. Readers have also linked it to his teaching, to wisdom and to baptism.
r: Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 17:13; Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Isaiah 12:3; Isaiah 55:1; 7:37–39; Revelation 22:1; Revelation 22:17

a: Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob?
p: The question expects "no." Readers know the answer is yes. The Jews ask the same about Abraham in 8:53.
b: The Greek form of the question expects the answer "no". John's readers know better: the one who saw angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man (1:51), as Jacob saw them at Bethel, is greater than Jacob. The same irony appears in 8:53 with Abraham. Calling Jacob "our father" is also a claim: the Samaritans saw themselves as true heirs of Jacob and Joseph.

p: Hallomai is used of people leaping, not usually of water. The water itself seems alive.
b: The verb hallomai means to jump or leap. It is used of the lame man leaping for joy (Acts 3:8) and, in the Greek Old Testament, of the Spirit rushing on Samson and Saul. Used of water it is unusual and vivid: a spring bubbling up inside the person. The water does not only satisfy thirst; it springs up toward eternal life, and in 7:38 it flows out from the believer to others.

p: Was she a sinful woman, a widow many times over, or a symbol of Samaria's history? Readers disagree.
b: Most readers through history took the woman as immoral, and Jesus' words as a gentle way of exposing her sin. But the text never calls her a sinner, and Jesus does not tell her to repent. Women could not usually divorce their husbands, so she may have been widowed or divorced several times, a tragedy rather than a scandal; the man she lived with now may have been a levirate partner or a protector who had not married her. Some scholars read the five husbands as a symbol of the five foreign peoples whose gods were brought into Samaria (2 Kings 17:24, 29–41; Josephus, Antiquities 9.288). Whatever her story, she becomes the first to bring a town to Jesus.

p: Samaritans did not accept the later prophets. To them "prophet" pointed to the one like Moses.
b: Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture. So they did not await a son of David, but the prophet God promised to Moses: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put my words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him" (Deuteronomy 18:18). Later Samaritan writings call him the Taheb, "the one who returns" or "restorer". The woman's words move step by step: a Jew (4:9), sir (4:11), a prophet (4:19), possibly the Messiah (4:29).

p: Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim, which towered over the well. Their copy of the Torah names it as God's chosen place.
b: From Jacob's well one looks up at Mount Gerizim. Moses had commanded that the blessings be spoken from Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and the Samaritan Pentateuch reads Deuteronomy 27:4 as "Gerizim" where the Jewish text has "Ebal". It also speaks of the place God "has chosen" (Deuteronomy 12:5) in the past tense, meaning Gerizim, while Jews took it to mean Jerusalem. Excavations on the summit have uncovered a large sacred precinct of the Persian and Hellenistic periods (whether the earliest phase had a temple building is debated). The temple there had lain in ruins for about 140 to 155 years when Jesus spoke, but Samaritans still worshiped on the mountain, as they do at Passover today.

p: A striking line in a Gospel often sharp toward "the Jews." Some think it was added later; most think it is central.
b: Jesus sides with Jewish worship: Samaritans worship what they do not know, since they reject the prophets and the Writings, while "we" (Jews) know. The Messiah comes from the Jewish people (Romans 9:5). Because this verse is so friendly to Jews in a Gospel that often speaks harshly of "the Jews" (8:44), Rudolf Bultmann judged it a later addition. Most scholars disagree: it shows that John's harsh language is a family quarrel, not a rejection of Israel. The Vatican's statement The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable (2015) and many Protestant statements on Jewish-Christian relations cite it.

p: Not "spiritual and sincere" in contrast with outward ritual, most think, but worship given by God's Spirit and centered on Jesus, the truth.
b: Some readers have taken "in spirit and truth" to mean inward worship from the heart, rather than outward ceremony or holy places. Quakers and some radical Reformation groups drew from it a worship without sacraments or set forms. Most commentators read it in John's own terms: "spirit" is God's Spirit, given through Jesus (3:5; 7:39), and "truth" is the reality God reveals in Jesus, who is "the truth" (14:6). The place of worship no longer matters, because God is met in Jesus, the new temple (2:21). The Dead Sea Scrolls also speak of God cleansing people with "a spirit of truth" (Community Rule, 1QS 4:20–21).

p: Not "a spirit," one among many, but a statement about God's nature, like "God is light" and "God is love."
b: Greek has no indefinite article, and "spirit" comes first for emphasis: God's very nature is spirit, not bound to a mountain or a building. The KJV's "God is a Spirit" can suggest one spirit among others. The statement belongs with "God is light" (1 John 1:5) and "God is love" (1 John 4:8). It does not mean God is distant, since the Word became flesh (1:14).

p: Samaritans looked for a figure like Moses who would reveal everything, not a king from David's line.
b: "Messiah" was a Jewish term; John translates it for his readers (as in 1:41). The woman's hope, that he "will announce all things to us", fits the Samaritan expectation of the Taheb, the prophet like Moses who would teach the truth and restore true worship. Josephus tells of a Samaritan who in AD 36 gathered followers on Mount Gerizim, promising to show them sacred vessels Moses had buried there; Pilate's troops crushed the gathering (Antiquities 18.85–87).

p: The Greek is simply "I am," the first of many "I am" sayings in John. Some hear God's own name in it.
b: Jesus says egō eimi, "I am", with "he" supplied in English. In ordinary Greek that means "It is I" or "I am the one." But John uses the phrase with special weight: seven times with an image ("I am the bread of life", 6:35), and several times alone (8:24, 28, 58; 13:19; 18:5–8). The Greek Old Testament used "I am" for God's self-naming in Isaiah (Isaiah 43:10; 46:4) and in Exodus 3:14. Here it first answers the woman plainly: I am the Messiah you are waiting for. Many readers hear more.

a: he was talking with a woman
p: Teachers were cautious about speaking with women in public. The disciples are shocked, but not enough to ask.
b: Some later rabbinic sayings warned against talking much with women, even one's own wife (Mishnah Avot 1:5). How strictly people kept to this in Jesus' day is debated, and Amy-Jill Levine and others warn against painting Jewish life as harsher to women than it was. Still, for a teacher to speak alone in public with an unknown woman, and a Samaritan, was unusual enough to surprise the disciples.

p: She came for water and left without it. Some read this as a sign that she found the living water.
b: The detail may simply show her haste. But many readers see a symbol: like the disciples who left their nets (Mark 1:18), she leaves behind what she came for, because she has found something better. The jar also recalls the stone water jars at Cana (2:6). She then acts as a witness: "Come and look" (4:29), the same invitation Philip gave Nathanael (1:46).

a: Four more months, and then the harvest
p: Probably a proverb about patience. If it is meant as a date, it would put this scene in winter.
b: In Palestine about four months passed between sowing grain (late autumn) and harvest (spring). The saying may be a proverb, "there is always time", or it may date the scene to around January. Either way, Jesus says the harvest is already here: the Samaritans coming across the fields are the crop, perhaps in their white clothes. In this harvest, sowing and reaping happen together, as the prophets said would happen in the days of renewal (Amos 9:13).

a: One person sows, and someone else harvests
p: A proverb usually meant as a complaint. Here it is good news: the disciples reap what others planted.
b: The saying sounds like a common proverb of unfairness (compare Deuteronomy 20:6; Micah 6:15). Jesus turns it around. But who are the "others" who did the hard work (4:38)? Jesus and the woman; John the Baptist (who may have baptized near Samaria, 3:23); the prophets before them; or, as many scholars read it, the early missionaries to Samaria, such as Philip (Acts 8:4–25), whose work the apostles Peter and John came to confirm (Acts 8:14).

p: A title given to emperors. The Samaritans, of all people, give it to Jesus.
b: "Savior" (sōtēr) was a title for gods and rulers. Inscriptions honored Julius Caesar, Augustus, Claudius and later Hadrian as "savior of the world" or "of the inhabited world". The Samaritans, outsiders to Judea's worship, now give it to Jesus, so the title means he is not only Israel's Messiah but the rescuer of all peoples (3:17). The phrase appears in the New Testament only here and in 1 John 4:14.
orig: ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου (ho sōtēr tou kosmou)

a: a prophet does not receive honor in his own homeland
p: Odd here, since Galilee welcomes him next. Is his homeland Galilee, Judea or Nazareth?
b: The other Gospels place this saying in Nazareth, where his own town rejected him (Mark 6:4; Matthew 13:57; Luke 4:24). In John it comes just as he is welcomed in Galilee (4:45). Readers explain it in three main ways. His "homeland" is Judea or Jerusalem, where he was born according to Matthew and Luke and which rejected him, so he leaves it. Or it is Galilee, and the welcome there is shallow, based only on signs (4:48). Or the "homeland" is "his own" people as a whole (1:11).

p: Likely a servant of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who was called "king" though he was not one.
b: Basilikos means "royal": a royal official, or possibly a soldier in the king's service. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who held the lesser title of tetrarch but was popularly called king (Mark 6:14). Capernaum, a border town on the lake, had officials, tax collectors and a garrison. The story resembles the healing of the centurion's servant in Matthew 8:5–13 and Luke 7:1–10: a man in Capernaum, a sick boy, a healing from a distance. Whether these are one event told two ways is debated.

a: If you people do not see signs and wonders
p: Jesus seems to rebuke the father. In John, faith that rests only on miracles is not yet enough.
b: The "you" is plural, addressed to Galileans in general (4:45). "Signs and wonders" is the common phrase for the miracles of the Exodus (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34). John has a double view of signs: they are meant to lead people to faith (2:11; 20:30–31), yet faith that depends on seeing marvels is shallow (2:23–25; 6:26). The official passes the test: he believes Jesus' word without seeing anything (4:50), and after the healing he "believed" in the full sense, with his household (4:53), like those who believe without seeing (20:29).

p: Doulos means slave, not just employee. Wealthy households in Galilee owned slaves.
b: Doulos is the ordinary Greek word for a slave, someone owned by another. Many English Bibles say "servant", which softens it. Slavery was common in the Roman world, including among wealthy Jewish households, though the Torah set limits on holding fellow Israelites (Leviticus 25:39–43). This translation says "slave" when doulos means a person owned by another, so that readers see the world of the text as it was. Jesus later uses the word of his followers, and tells them he calls them friends instead (15:15).

p: About one in the afternoon. The man did not get home until the next day, though Cana was only a day's walk.
b: Counted from sunrise, the seventh hour is about 1 p.m. From either proposed site of Cana to Capernaum is some 15 or 16 miles (25 km), mostly downhill, a long day's walk. The father met his slaves "yesterday" by their reckoning, which suggests he did not hurry home, as if he trusted Jesus' word, or that he stayed the night on the way. The detail matters to the story: the boy was healed at the very hour Jesus spoke.

p: John numbers only the first two signs. Some think he used an older "Book of Signs."
b: Jesus has done other signs in Jerusalem (2:23), yet this one is called "the second", counting from Cana (2:11). Both happen in Cana after Jesus comes from Judea. Rudolf Bultmann and Robert Fortna argued that John drew on an earlier written source, a "Signs Gospel", which numbered the miracles, and that the numbering survived though other signs were added in between. Others think John counts only the Cana signs, to frame chapters 2–4 as a unit from Cana to Cana.
